ca_navarro_beach.blurb: A single sandstone boulder on the beach in Navarro River Redwoods State Park, on the Mendocino coast south of the Highway 128 junction. It stands roughly 20 feet tall, though the sand around its base rises and falls with the seasons, so it can look like a mere bump one visit and a proper highball the next. The ten problems here are bouldering lines, mostly easy, with a few much harder ones mixed in. The landing is flat, soft sand, but holds can be loose or crusted with grit, so test them. It is a quiet coastal stop rather than a destination session.

ca_charlatan_the.blurb: A formation within the Needles, the cluster of spires above the Kern River Valley in Sequoia National Forest in the southern Sierra. It sits at roughly 7,900 feet, directly above the Sorcerer and the first big formation past the Magician. Nearly everything here is trad, from a short fifth-class scramble up the odd blocky summit to multi-pitch crack and face lines, with grades running from 5.7 up to the low 5.12s and the bulk in the 5.10s and 5.11s. A lone boulder problem rounds out the ten climbs. Routes can be reached from the main trail on either side.

ca_super_slab.blurb: A small bouldering spot on the Sonoma Coast, just north of Jenner along Highway 1 inside Sonoma Coast State Park. The schist blocks hold ten problems that split between easy lines at about V0 and a run of hard low sit starts and traverses reaching into the V7 and V8 range, with a few mid-grade problems between. The walk from the road is about a minute, so a session here is quick and simple, and it makes an easy add-on to a day of coastal bouldering at the neighbouring sectors of the park.

ca_sunshine_boulder.blurb: A single boulder in the roadside Buttermilks Main zone near Bishop, in the Eastern Sierra, sitting a short uphill hike northwest of the Grandma Peabody Boulder. The ten problems are all bouldering and all on the easy side: one VB, mostly V0, and a few V1s, with the southeast face offering a steep slab and the best lines. The north side is more of a down-climb. It suits beginners, warm-ups and kids, and is a calm stop within the very busy Buttermilks.

ca_uptown_rock_upper_tier.blurb: The top tier of Uptown Rock, a big formation in Pine Creek Canyon above Bishop in the Eastern Sierra. The climbing is smooth, featured slab and face, mostly moderate, running from about 5.5 up to a single 5.10, with the bulk in the 5.8 range. Seven of the ten routes are trad and three are sport; the bolts tend to be spaced farther apart than at typical Pine Creek sport crags, so expect technical, balancy movement rather than pump. This tier is usually sheltered from the wind and feels warm, though it can turn chilly late in the day in spring. A small-to-medium rack covers the gear routes.

ca_hailstone_rock.blurb: A sub-area of the Satellite Rocks high on Mount St. Helena, in the Wine Country north of the Bay Area. Ten routes, seven of them sport and three trad, mostly in the 5.9 to 5.11 range with a couple of easier lines. The routes are long and tall and many look out over big views. The approach is the real commitment: a steep, brushy uphill hike of an hour or more with a fixed rope on one section, so it is no place for dogs. Because the fragile slopes erode easily, this rock sees fewer visitors than the nearby Bubble and Bear Cliff.

ca_talon.blurb: A small sport crag at the High Eagle area on Shuteye Ridge, in the western Sierra off Highway 41 near Fresno Dome, at about 7,300 feet. Of its ten routes, nine are bolted and one is a top-rope line, with grades from one easy 5.7 up through a main run of 5.10s and 5.11s and a single 5.12. It sits right beside the rough 4WD road that leaves the camp, so the walk is almost nothing. The crag gets morning shade, which is unusual for this part of Shuteye, and it makes a handy warm-up before heading to the longer lines at High Eagle.
